newsitem.title: CUBA: FEATURE - Music links Havana's present to vanished past.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Music links Havana's present to vanished past.

text.p: Before the revolution, the planes would ply back and forth across the Florida straits, carrying American jazz musicians to perform in Havana, then taking them back to play the same night in Miami's swanky beachfront hotels.

Nearly 40 years later, the flights from Miami to Havana have gone, along with the time of creative ferment when jazz first met Cuban music to spawn a host of new sounds -- jazz with a Latin beat, Cuban standards with a jazz feeling.

Cuban pianist Frank Emilio Flynn, a veteran of those days, plays in a dollars-only restaurant that is too expensive for most Cubans, with no audience but his son, a single visitor and several idle waiters. He still recalls the fertile 1950s encounters between Latin musicians and American jazzmen at clubs such as La Habana 1900 that led him and others to pioneer those new styles.

"They didn't get paid, the only thing necessary was of course to pay for their air fare and their stay ... we had the chance to play with Philly Joe Jones, others," Flynn told Reuters. "They would come and after playing often they would go back to play there (in Miami) at night in the hotels ... there was enthusiasm, we would do jam sessions, there was a lot of interchange, above all at the jazz club, there was the possibility of direct contact with them and they were interested in that syncretism," he said.
"Dizzie Gillespie had done some of this in the United States, but here we were among the pioneers," he added of his ground-breaking Modern Cuban Music Instrumental Quintet.
FREE-FORM CREATIVE CONTACT

That free-form creative contact in jam-packed Havana nightspots died off after the 1959 Cuban revolution and the U.S. embargo against President Fidel Castro's Communist regime. Black-and-white photographs in hotels such as the now state-run Hotel Nacional de Cuba give a glimpse of the days when mobsters held sway in Havana and artists such as Frank Sinatra and Ava Gardner would hit town.

The embargo greatly curtails the ability of U.S. musicians, as well as all other citizens, to travel to Cuba, although some attend formal state-sponsored music festivals. U.S. officials say the embargo is vital to pressure Castro to adopt economic and political reforms.

Musical contacts continue though. Many Cuban musicians travel to the United States and other countries; some have sought asylum and chosen not to return to Castro's Cuba, while others faithfully go back.
Few of those who still live in Cuba play Miami, though.

Hardline members of Miami's powerful anti-Castro Cuban community accuse them of propping up the Communist regime with the dollars from their tours. A Miami radio station recently had to stop playing music by the popular Cuban band Los Van Van after receiving threats and a restaurant that was planning to present a singer who lives in Havava was firebombed.
NO POLITICAL CONTENT

"It Is sad," Juan Formell, the founder and leader of Los Van Van, told Reuters at Havana airport after returning from a brief tour of southeastern Mexico. "We don't do politics in our music, our music is for dancing, it is popular Cuban music with no political content at all."
He said some Miami Cubans, intent upon hearing Los Van Van, made the trip to Cancun in the Mexican Caribbean to hear them play recently at the resort's Bar Azucar.

Chucho Valdes, a leading Cuban musician who is about to embark on a U.S. and European tour omitting Miami, said he had not been invited to play there but would do so like a shot if asked. "I have received no invitation but if I am asked I will go, surely, surely, surely," he told Reuters.
Informal contact also persists between Cuban musicians caught on either side of the ideological divide.

Formell said he was a friend of the owner of Cafe Nostalgia in Miami's Little Havana district, which, between sets of Cuban music, shows black-and-white film of musicians of pre-revolutionary Havana such as singer Rita Montaner and band leader Benny More.
MUSICIANS STAY IN TOUCH

Flynn, one of the elder statesmen of Cuban music, also said musicians who have chosen to stay in the United States remain in touch with him, telephoning him regularly from Miami. "We are not to blame for these things," he said of what he called "the discrepancy" between Castro's Cuba and the United States. "We always kept ourselves apart from them."

Flynn, now 76 and blind since youth, asked the floor of the virtually empty La Roca restaurant for requests and then slid into elegant, restrained versions of his own music and classics from the Cuban, jazz and classical repertoire.

He recalled New Year's Eve 1958 in Havana, when corrupt and brutal President Fulgencio Batista fled into exile ahead of Castro's advancing guerrillas and Cubans woke up to find 1959 had brought them a new government, one that many would later flee.

"Fortunately, that night I finished early, at 10 p.m.," he said. "The Comodoro hotel was something, you could already feel the heavy atmosphere, there was hardly any audience. I had no idea what was going to happen and I got a surprise when I woke up and found that things had taken another course.
"We carried on playing our jazz, to the extent that in the middle of the revolution we recorded albums."

Frail and shuffling but perfectly lucid despite his years, Flynn said threats against those fostering access to music from Castro's Cuba did not scare him and he would be delighted to play Miami. "I am not afraid," he said.
